keyVerseText: And he said unto them, Go ye, and tell that fox, Behold, I cast out devils, and I do cures to day and to morrow, and the third day I shall be perfected.
rootMeaning: The Greek noun ἴασις (íasis) derives from the verb ἰάομαι (iáomai), which means to heal or make whole, either literally or figuratively. This root emphasizes not just the cessation of symptoms but the restoration of full health and wholeness. Unlike the simple English term 'heal,' the root conveys an active process of curing or remedying, highlighting the transformative power inherent in true healing.
usageInScripture: The word ἴασις appears three times in the New Testament, consistently conveying the concept of healing or cures. It is translated primarily as 'cures,' 'of healing,' and 'heal,' reflecting both the act and result of restoration. This consistency in usage underscores its specific theological focus on divine intervention that brings about physical or spiritual renewal, as seen in Luke 13:32 where Jesus speaks of performing cures.
theologicalSignificance: Understanding ἴασις enriches our grasp of God's restorative work through Christ. It is not merely about alleviating suffering but about the comprehensive healing that God brings—body, soul, and spirit. This word roots the Christian faith in the hope of divine healing as a sign of the Kingdom breaking into the present age. Recognizing ἴασις as a mode of healing reminds believers that Christ’s ministry involved active restoration and that such healing points forward to ultimate redemption and perfection in Him.
keyVerseReflection: In Luke 13:32, Jesus declares, 'I cast out devils, and I do cures to day and to morrow, and the third day I shall be perfected.' The use of ἴασις here highlights Jesus’ ongoing work of healing as a sign of His messianic authority and mission. It emphasizes not only the physical cures but also the spiritual restoration He brings, affirming that His work of healing is integral to His redemptive purpose, culminating in His resurrection and perfection on the third day.
